finding.claim: Mass assignment on PUT /me: the whole request body is merged into the authenticated user object and persisted, so any user can set arbitrary fields such as role, isAdmin, id, email-verified flags or tenant/org ids, enabling privilege escalation or account takeover. The sibling route PUT /me/profile (line 11) whitelists only displayName and bio, which shows the intended behaviour.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled JSON body of an authenticated PUT /me request (req.body)
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) followed by req.store.save(req.user) persisting the modified user record

trace.note: PUT /me handler; no field filtering or validation middleware visible in this file
Object.assign copies every body property onto req.user, including privileged fields
Updated user is returned in the response

finding.guards_checked: Only one file exists in the repo. There is no allowlist, schema validation or authorization middleware in it. The sibling /me/profile route explicitly destructures displayName and bio, which contrasts with this one. Authentication middleware that sets req.user is not present in the repo, so I could not verify it. Even if it exists, it only authenticates the user and does not restrict which fields they can write. __proto__ assignment through Object.assign is not a prototype-pollution issue, because it only sets the prototype of req.user and does not modify Object.prototype.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 does Object.assign(req.user, req.body) and users.js:6 saves it with no field allowlist or validation, unlike the whitelisted /me/profile at users.js:11-12, so any authenticated user can write privileged fields on their own record.
